subtopic: ADMISSION OF GERMANY AS PERMANENT MEMBER OF COUNCIL

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: ADMISSION OF GERMANY AS PERMANENT MEMBER OF COUNCIL
speechtext:
Next week there is to be a meeting of the council of the League of Nations at Geneva and a special meeting of the assembly for the purpose of making Germany a permanent member of the council of the league. At present the council consists of four permanent members and six other members selected by the assembly from time to time. I see by the press that an effort may be made at this meeting in Geneva to further increase the permanent members of the council, but this cannot be
fMr. New-bum.]
done without the approval of the assembly. I should like to ask the acting head of the government the names of the delegates who will represent Canada on this occasion, whether any, and if so, what instructions have been given them regarding the admission ot Germany to the council and also regarding the question of further increasing the permanent members of the council in case it comes up for discussion in the assembly.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Leader of the House):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMISSION OF GERMANY AS PERMANENT MEMBER OF COUNCIL
speechtext:
As my hon. friend has said, the
Secretary General of the League of Nations has requested the various members of the league to send delegates to a special meeting of the assembly to be held on March 8 for the purpose of considering the request of Germany for admission to the council of the league. The Canadian delegates are Senator Dandurand, leader in the Senate, who was president of the assembly last fall, the High Commissioner for Canada in London and the Commissioner for Canada in Paris, with Dr. Riddell, who is already in Geneva, as a substitute. It seems to be the general opinion everywhere that Germany should be admitted as a member of the league, and even given a seat on the council. As my hon. friend has said, proposals have been made for the appointment, as permanent members of the council, of two or three other nations, Spain, Brazil and Poland having been suggested. The matter was discussed with Senator Dandurand prior to his departure for Geneva, but of course whatever may be my opinion or the opinion of other hon. members it is preferable that the formal applications of these nations be placed before the assembly before any private views are expressed in regard to them. It is understood that communications will be exchanged between our representatives there and this government, but the'matter of making public all the information that may come to the government is, I think, somewhat delicate. I have noticed, as hon. gentlemen may have noticed also, that both in England and in France the government have declined to state their opinion on the matter at the present time. My hon. friend may be sure that the views expressed in Canada by those who are especially interested in questions appertaining to the League of Nations, the views of such organizations, for example, as the League of Nations Association, as well as of private individuals, will be given the most serious consideration. If I were free I might say that my opinion coincides with that of my hon. friend, but I am not free to say so. However, everything will be submitted to the delegates there and the views of Canada will be represented.

Excessive Moisture in Grain
On the Orders of the Day:

On
January 22 I drew the attention of the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce to the fact that owing to congestion in the elevator at Fort William a considerable quantity of damp grain was likely to spoil. I want to ask now what special measures have been adopted by the department to prevent loss of western gyain because of excessive moisture, and what progress has been made.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This morning my hon.
friend advised me that he would ask this question, so that I am in a position to put on Hansard a statement of the measures which the government have taken to take care of damp and tough grain in elevators and in transit. After my hon. friend on January 22 had directed our attention to the serious situation on account of the large amount of tough and damp grain on hand, and following the statement I then made, I obtained a report from the chairman of the grain commission, dated January 28, who advised me that a statement prepared that day showed that of 5,000 cars in the yards at the head of the lakes the Canadian Pacific Railway had 87 with damp and 1,177 with tough grain; and the Canadian National 170 with damp and 923 with tough grain. He further advised me that the terminal elevators were picking [DOT]out the damp cars billed to them so that they might be taken in and dried. He assured me that every effort was being made to take care of tough and damp grain so as to minimize the danger of loss.
Following that, on February 20, the secretary of the grain commission, in a letter directed to the Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce, advised the department on the situation. In order that the House and the country may have the benefit of this information, I crave indulgence to place the letter on Hansard:
Dear Sir:
Tough and Damp Grain
Owing to the large amount of tough and damp grain now in store in public and private elevators throughout the western grain inspection division, as well as considerable quantities in transit railway yards, country elevators and in farmers' hands, the board had several meetings with interested parties regarding the drying of this grain.
The drying facilities throughout the western inspection division are practically all operating to their full capacity in the drying of damp grain, with the result that most of the damp grain now in store in the elevators will be dried before the opening of navigation.
Under the provisions of the tariff governing the public terminal elevators operating in the western inspection division, tough grain is received from November 1 to April 1 under the same terms and conditions applying to straight grade grains. Such tough grain, therefore, as may be in store at the present time-must be allowed to remain in store in its present, condition, unless it should become heated, in which event sections of the act relating to out-of-condition* grain (130 to 139) must be complied with.
After reviewing the whole situation very carefully the board is of the opinion that all tough and damp grain now in store in the elevators can be taken care of, providing the drying of same is proceeded with immediately, the elevators equipped with drying facilities utilizing same to their full capacity, but there is a danger of the grain now in box cars, both in transit and in railway yards, and that yet to be marketed, going out of condition, if we should experience an early spring.
At the present time the elevators have sufficient tough and damp grain in store to keep their drying facilities working to full capacity continuously from March 1 to the opening of navigation.
The only way in which the drying facilities can be used to the best advantage is to allow the public and private elevators to dry, with the least possible delay, all tough 3 northern and lower grades of wheat now in store, and in addition all tough, coarse grains as may be advisable, so that these facilities will be available at the opening of navigation to take care of grain which is in danger of going out of condition and which cannot be unloaded at the present time.
The board's reason for recommending the drying of only 3 northern and lower grades of wheat is that under section 96 of the Canada Grain Act, the last paragraph under the heading, "Spring Wheat", 3 northern and lower grades which may be dried, may be graded in such regular grades as the inspector determines, whereas, in the drying of 1 and 2 northern, the inspector, in his discretion, issues a certificate for dried 1 or 2 northern, which only commands the price of 3 northern wheat.
Then, on the recommendation of the Board of Grain Commissioners, this order in council was passed on February 26:
The following regulations made by the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada, pursuant to sections 20, 87 and 140 of the Canada Grain Act, chapter 33, 15-16 George V, are hereby approved:
(1)	All public and private elevators in the western grain inspection division, except those public and private elevators situated at Vancouver, shall proceed to dry, according to the drying facilities in the elevators in which such grain may be stored, all tough 3 northern and lower grades of tough wheat, and, in addition, all tough, coarse grains as may be advisable.
(2)	On all tough grain dried, the elevator^ shall be entitled to deduct 4 per cent from the amount as shown on the outstanding warehouse receipt to cover loss in drying.
(3) This order in council shall be effective the Jirst day of March, 1926, and shall be subject to such regulations as the board may provide under subsection 1 of section 87 of the Canada Grain Act, to ensure the proper carrying out of this order.
(4) The Board of Grain Commissioners, owing to the urgency of the situation, is empowered to make regulations for the handling of such tough and damp grain, under the provisions of section 87, effective on the publication of such regulations, without requiring to submit such regulations for the approval of the Governor in Council.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Leader of the House):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this House has been sitting since the seventh day of January. It was summoned at the earliest possible date after the general election for a special purpose, namely to settle the situation created by that election. On November 17 the Prime Minister (Mr. King) issued a statement giving the reasons why parliament had been summoned for that date, and I am going to read just a few words from that statement. He said:
Once the question of party majority is settled, an adjournment of parliament can be made to enable whichever party may be entrusted with the duty of carrying on the government time within which to conduct the necessary by-elections and have in readiness the further work of the session.
He also added:
The interests of the country will therefore in no way suffer if, as soon as parliament meets, the question of majority support is decided and an adjournment is then made to permit of the party enjoying the support of the majority dn the House of Commons making the necessary arrangements for .the continuance at the proper time of the work of the session.
It was well understood and discussed in the press all over Canada that when this question was settled there would be an adjournment of the House for the purpose already mentioned. On the 8th of January, the day following the opening of parliament, the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) challenged the right of the government to summon parliament and carry on the administration. This motion was voted down after a somewhat extensive debate, and on the 18th of January the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott) moved the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. This debate went on for a certain time, and on the 26th of January, when the debate was being adjourned, the right hon. leader of the opposition, as may be seen in Hansard at page 473, said:
While this motion is not debatable, certainly we ought to be closing this debate and not dragging it along at such great length with such extended speeches.
The right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), on the 28th of January, as will be seen at page 496 of Hansard, inquired

The Address-Mr. Lapointe
from the government whether it was true that there would be an adjournment of the House, and he added:
The consequence of the intimations has been that members of this House have not been able to make their arrangements for the session, ot the bringing down of members of their families who intend to be here should the session be continued. There has been a constant disarrangement of the programme of very many hon. members of parliament. I thank the government should intimate now-in fact it should have done so sooner- whether it proposes to ask for an adjournment of the House for any considerable period of time; if so for what period, and when.
Answering my right hon. friend I said, for the purpose of his friends making their arrangements accordingly, that there would be an adjournment of six weeks, and that a motion would be presented to the House for that purpose. A notice of motion was immediately given, and on January 28th, when the debate was adjourned, my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (,Mr. Stevens), who was then leading the opposition, said:
Mr. Speaker, I would 'like to ask the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) as leader of the House how long it is intended to prolong this debarte and, I may say, obstruct the progress of business. Can my hon. friend give to the House any indication of when we may expect it to close, in order that hon. members may adjust themselves to this rather strange and unusual position of a government obstructing its own business?
Belying on these statements, Mr. Speaker, a motion was presented to the House for the purpose of securing an adjournment of parliament for a period of six weeks, 'but immediately this motion came before the House it was fought and opposed from all angles by hon. gentlemen opposite. Still it was voted on and approved by a majority of the members of this House. Then hon. gentlemen opposite, instead of voting the Address, as they had appeared so anxious to do, resumed the debate, and my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), on February the 8th, one month after the opening of parliament, moved an amendment which would have had its proper place in the budget debate. That amendment was voted down, and my hon. friend from Nelson (Mr. Bird) then moved the previous question.
In the course of the debate on the motion of my hon. friend from Nelson, as well as on the motion of my hon. friend from South Oxford, we heard statements at different times from hon. gentlemen opposite that they would debate this Address and would speak as long as was necessary to prevent an adjournment being granted. I say, Sir, that this was frustrating the will of parliament; it was treating with contempt the decision of the majority and the supremacy of this legislative body. 
Hon. gentlemen opposite refer to us in terms of contempt as a remnant of a government.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hear, hear. They know those words have been repeated every day. The terms do not change very much. The government is described as a remnant of a government, as a rump, or a trunk and other expressions of that kind; but, Sir, such as it is, this remnant, this rump, this trunk, has beaten hon. gentlemen opposite every time we have been given the opportunity, and this has happened on eight different occasions this session-and nine, if I include the vote this afternoon. Obviously they do not seem to realize that when they belittle opponents who beat them at every corner and at every opportunity, they but accentuate and demonstrate and exhibit their own weakness. They have lost their own time; they have lost our time, and they have lost the time of the country. They could not defeat the government. I challenge them to defeat us now; they cannot defeat us.
Wait till the next election.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Wait till the next election? But we are in parliament just now. This is the explanation, Mr. Speaker, why we have been so tolerant, so patient, allowing the opposition of hon. gentlemen opposite to wear itself out, to disappear of -itself, of its own futility and meaninglessness. But, Mr. Speaker, the statement made by the chief whip of the (Conservative party
4 p.m. (Mr. Boys) on Friday afternoon was a bold and brazen challenge which we cannot ignore. The majority of the members of this House must rule, and the majority of the members of this House will rule. The will of the majority of parliament has been asserted in two main and glaring instances. First, it declared that the government was justified in summoning parliament and in carrying on the administration; second, that this parliament should adjourn for a certain -period of time for -the purposes which were submitted to the House.
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, I have only ten
minutes more. My right hon. friend knows well the rules of which he is the father.
The attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite has been one of contempt for parliamentary institutions, and they have the unenviable responsibility for the feeling in the minds of

The Address-Mr. Lapointe
*many people which such contempt spreads throughout the country. I was sorry when I heard my eminent friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) use in the course of his speech the following words:
I can tell him that so fair as I am concerned, he will have to change the rules of the House to prevent my obstructing, in order to prevent the forcing through of any such measure as that.
I was sorry for my hon. friend, for whom I have the greatest respect and admiration, 'because that statement was certainly not worthy of his high reputation. What are laws and what are regulations if not an expression of the will of the majority? And it is setting a pernicious example and giving a nefarious excuse to would-be lawbreakers when political leaders challenge the will of majority and try to smuggle through their own defeated persons and opinions.
Last year a committee sat for the purpose of revising the rules of parliament, and one of the decisions of that committee was that the length of speeches in this House should be restricted to forty minutes, except those of the two leaders. That recommendation was unanimously adopted by the committee ana reported to the House. The leader of the opposition, when the report came up in the House, said that unfortunately it came up too late in the session, but he was giving his support to those rules, and he would see to it that they would carry after the election.
What?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My right hon. friend may deny the statement but he can read Hansard. I will not cite any newspaper extracts. If that was his opinion, what can we say about my right hon. friend who resorts to tactics that he himself thought should be suppressed? What is to be thought of the logic of the statement of the chief whip of the opposition when he said: We are prolonging this debate because there is no business before the House. We will wait untif the Prime Minister is back in the House and if he has no business after one day or two days, we will vote and we will adjourn. We will cease obstruction, for the very reason for which we obstructed. Have you ever seen such logic? I was not surprised that the chief whip seemed uneasy when he was reading that carefully prepared statement which had been placed in his hands. How can it be otherwise when statesmanship, broad vision and public interest are to give way to spite, disappointment and narrow partisanship? The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George discovered something else. He said: The acting leader of the government is responsible because he made a motion for the purpose of giving precedence to the Address. Let him withdraw that motion and proceed with business. Is that Tory loyalty when those gentlemen are out of power? When has the House refrained from moving the Address for the purpose of discussing the legislation announced in the Speech from the Throne? It is the first communication of the sovereign and it is always given first consideration. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) (sited a case in 1884 when the consideration of the Address was postponed from day to day on account of a vote of censure regarding affairs in the Soudan war. This was so exceptional that Bourinot and May have recorded it. In the same way this year something exceptional was moved in this chamber before the Address was considered. It was the motion of my hon. friend. In the British House of Commons the Address is voted after a very few days of debate. In 1882 the British House of Commons considered the Address from February 7' to February 18, and it is the longest ease recorded in Bourinot. It is preposterous on the part of gentlemen who have a standing in this House to suggest that the Address be withdrawn for the purpose of considering the legislation announced in the Speech from the Throne. Before the Address is voted the House is not properly organized to function. We have no Deputy Speaker, and you, Sir, have been a martyr to your duty as Speaker.
I repeat, the majority in this House is going to rule. We are not those who can be intimidated or discouraged. The majority of the people of Canada, whether you call them Liberals, Progressives, Labour or Independents, have intimated that they do not want the right hon. gentleman as Prime Minister of Canada and we shall see to it that their will is respected and that my right hon. friend does not reach the goal of his ambition. Hon. gentlemen have wasted nearly two months in futile, dull, uninteresting debate, and if I may be permitted, with all due deference, I may say a debate prolific only of abuse, denunciations and very feeble, auxiliary gibes and jokes. The power to decide is in the hands, not of those whom my right hon. friend would like to have as judges, but of those whom the people have elected as judges. His argument is based on what should be done. My argument is based on what has been done.
Since the date of the general elections, the Conservative party has gone through three successive periods. First we witnessed a

The Address-Mr. Meighen
Niagara of vehement enthusiasm which gradually decreased in intensity; second, we were subjected to bitter criticism, sometimes verging on insanity, and, third, some gentlemen of the Conservative party-I do not mean in the House-have suffered from an epidemic of political hysteria. The frenzy of part of the Tory press of Canada to-day is the comic relief of our current politics. Let me tell them once and for aill that we are not going to let anybody shout us out, or abuse us out, or even chloroform us out by meaningless and tiresome speeches. We are going to carry on this administration in the interest of all the people in Canada and not merely of some private business. Many forces are exerting themselves against us and are resorting to spectacular publicity. They are active in our province, but we are there blocking the way and we dare them and their plutocratic methods to defeat us. While they are whining and whistling, Canada is going aheau, Canada is entering upon a new period of not only recovery 'but of prosperity, as all the statistics of trade, employment and public finance demonstrate eloquently. We are going to carry on; we are going to appeal to the best, not to the worst of men, not to their hatreds or their passions. We are going to appeal to unity and harmony in this country, and we shall be victorious.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
The acting leader of
the government has delivered himself, I hope to his own satisfaction, of a speech evidently quite carefully prepared over a long period of time-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is another one of the right hon. member's mistakes.

the purpose of which, so far as I could judge, was to crowd as many of the offences which he charged against us as could possibly be crowded into the compass of his own twenty minute speech. In the course of his preparation there was one resource which he very distinctly omitted. While emphasizing the dfetermination of his government, which he himself calls a trunk, a chunk and I know not what, to carry on by force of majority-which, by the way, is not its party's majority at all-he became very enthusiastic over the rule which he now invokes. Hon. members who were within parliament prior to four years ago will remember that, of all hou. gentlemen opposite in numbers then almost what they are to-day who condemned this rule, its principle, its initiation, its application, who condemned it day and night with bell,

book and candle, the most vociferous was himself the then hon. member for Kamouraska. He declared that the application ofj this rule was the gag and the disruption of a free parliament. As time is very precious I cannot quote much of what he said. If I could quote . it all, I would piece together from the speeches of the then hon. member for Kamouraska, the present Minister of Justice, a better speech than he delivered this afternoon but one wholly on the other side of the case. He said on the 16th April, 1913, when this very rule was under review:
I wish to enter my solemn protest on behalf of my constituents which I have the honour to represent in this House against this infamous proposal of the government.
This infamous proposal which he now adopts as his own in the House to-day:
When I hand over my mandate to .them, I will be in a position to say: "You are free citizens and you have returned a free representative; I was desirous of fulfilling niv duty, my whole duty; but it happened one day that brute foroe prevented me from doing so, I was gagged.
Who is the parent of brute force this afternoon? Who is the gagger now? He continued :
But, Mr. Speaker, .there still remains with us two sources of energy which cannot be gagged; faith in the righteousness of our cause and the nobleness of o>ur aims.
At another point he declared that by this rule parliament had debased itself and that mails or mail bags could be robbed, and all sorts . of 'crimes could be committed. The people's representatives could never intervene; the freedom of parliament was gone. The hon. member was not alone in that respect. The hon. member who now sits behind him stood up and in a voice fulll of pathos declared that he was sorry to have to admit that he rose for the last time in a free parliament, that parliament had been robbed of functions of which it had boasted for generations. There was scarcely an hon. gentleman 'opposite, indeed not one of those who were in the House at that time, who did not denounce the closure rule, denounce its principle, its application and everything about it, and declared that it was alien to British institutions. One after another rose in his place and said: "The Conservatives want to restrict trade and now also they want to restrict discussion. We are for freedom on both counts of the indictment, and in the cause of freedom we are prepared to suffer and die." The hon. member will recall those words from the mouth of the then member for Red Deer, who excelled in eloquence, if not in vituperation, those who represent the Liberal party

The Address-Mr. Meighen
to-day. Now they have abandoned both free trade and free discussion.
I do not object to closure. I believe the closure rule is essential in all free parliaments. This doctrine I preached in 1913, and this doctrine we on this side of the House sought to drive home to hon. members opposite. This doctrine they repudiated and they declared that parliament debased itself by the adoption of such a rule. Has any explanation come from the Minister of Justice this afternoon of his change of front? Is there anything left for this government to swallow of all its professions throughout all its history?
The closure rule has been open to adoption by hon. gentlemen opposite from the beginning. By the rules of the House we always loyally abide. By this rule, as by every other rule, we are prepared to abide. What is to be thought of a leader of the government who, afraid to use the rule, afraid to resort to perfectly proper remedies at his disposal, sits in his seat for days and weeks, and complains of members on this side of the House?
The hon. minister comes forward and tell3 us, "Oh, we just called parliament together on the 7th January for one purpose and only one purpose, namely, to find out which party had the confidence of parliament, whether the government of the day or some other party. Is that why they called parliament? Does toe leader of the government reaffirm now his statement that that is why he called parliament together? He told us when parliament met that such was the reason. Why then did he put a long succession of misrepresentation and deceit in the mouth of His Excellency in the form of an Address, if parliament was called together for the sole purpose of deciding who was supreme in parliament? If the minister now speaks the truth, that purpose should have been the sole constituent in the Speech of His Excellency presented to the House of Commons. That was what ought to have been the sole feature of the Speech, but the hon. gentleman knew that if he came honestly before this House and stated the purpose of calling the session he could not get a majority in this House. The hon. members knew that on the record of their four years they could not get a majority in the House, and the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) admitted this truth in one of the debates in the House this session. After all these blandishments have been held out by way of bribe and nothing else to hon. members to my left-matters that were entirely foreign to the purpose of calling parliament together-the Minister of Customs, speaking for the government, knowing well that on their record they could not be
sustained, looked across to hon. members to my left and said:	"If you vote with us on
this vote of confidence you do not vote support of us or approval of us on our record." And furthermore, he declared that the government would not accept the vote as one of confidence entitling them to the rights of a government at all. By that assertion a farcical and artificial loophole was offered to hon. gentlemen, through which they could escape and through which they could, to the. satisfaction to the government at least, justify the support of the administration. By virtue of such conduct they have gathered round them the support, temporarily, I hope, of the hon. members to my left, and not one of those hon. members will rise in 'his place now and say that for any other reason on earth he supports this government at this time.
This government, the moment they faced a motion of confidence, declared that those who Would vote for them would not be voting confidence in them at all. On the assertion of the Minister of Customs on behalf of the government it was to be no vote of confidence. Can any member of the .government dare say that parliament has voted confidence in them to this day? The government is directing its efforts now to see that the House gets no opportunity to vote on the question of confidence. The government invokes what it declared for ten years to be an infamous closure rule, in order to make sure that parliament never gets an opportunity of voting want' of confidence. In this they have the co-operation" of at least certain hon. members to my left. In this they have the active "co-operation" of the hon member for Nelson (Mr. Bird). After resolutions expressive of what we believed to be fundamental faults in government policy were disposed of, this House was about to have presented to it, as hon. gentlemen knew, as the hon. member for Nelson knew, as every member of the Progressive party knew-
No, no.

The hon. gentleman did not
know any such thing.

The hon. gentleman
from Nelson did not know what?

Did not know what the right
hon. leader of the opposition -alleges.

The leader of the opposition has not stated yet what the hon. member for Nelson knew. He rose before I said it. This was part of the "co-operation." Through the press of this country we had informed this House -more than once that a vote

The Address-Mr. Meighen
of want of confidence would be moved, and even the name of the mover was given to the press. If hon. gentlemen did not know it, then they are using the word "know" in a sense never before understood in parliament. Right on the eve of the motion, when indeed the member who was about to make the motion was on his feet, the member for Nelson stood up and forced himself on the attention of the Speaker, in order that what we are told was the avowed purpose of calling parliament might be frustrated; in order that hon. gentlemen would not be in the position of having to vote yes or no on the question of confidence. The debate has been prolonged, so hon. members opposite complain. They say that as long ago as January 28 or early in Februa-ary I asked why the government did not get on with business. Certainly I did, and I have asked that question ever since. We on this side have appealed to the government to bring some business before parliament. We have offered, and the government has known that we have been prepared all these weeks, to come to a vote on the Address provided only there was some business for parliament to transact.
The closure rule is all right; it is perfectly defensible, justifiable and necessary. But never in the history of any parliament was closure adopted for the purpose of giving its members a holiday. Those who stoutly resisted this rule when applied only for the purpose of learning the will of parliament on absolutely essential legislation, only for the purpose of getting the decision of this House on important legislation submitted by the government; those who fought day and night to prevent the application of closure for such purpose, come into parliament this afternoon and call upon all their own followers and their allies to the left to stand up and support closure in order that parliament may adjourn.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Support parliament.
Support closure, in order that parliament may adjourn. The Minister of the Interior does not like the expression because it is the truth. Now what position is the government in?
A good position.

The government is in a good position just as a criminal about to be electrocuted is in a good position when he takes the chair.
Serious charges are to-day levelled against the administration. Serious charges are under review before a committee of this House; seri-

ous charges have been levelled across the floor in respect of malfeasance of office by this administration. And while one set of these charges are under review by a committee of parliament this government forces closure in order that the work of that committee may be rendered null and void. This parliament, at the instance of the government, denudes ' that committee of all power to enforce its decisions; it leaves the committee stranded and helpless without our moral support and at the mercy of witnesses who may defy its will. For this purpose closure is applied. Charges of defiance of parliament have been levelled against the administration supported by indisputable evidence, supported by their own orders in council-a defiance of parliament as illegal, as utterly indefensible, as brazen as anything that any government in any country in the world ever dared to perpetrate. These charges have not even met with a meed of attempted defence at the hands of any member of the government; and while the administration is in that position its leader rises and, without offering any defence whatever, calls upon a majority in this House, composed of his supporters and his allies, to vote parliament into an adjournment while they themselves proceed with the project which they have undertaken by means of these illegal steps and in contempt of the will of this House.
Is this parliament to sit idly by as a mere spectator while the government dips its hands into the treasury and takes out millions for the execution of projects which parliament has never authorized and does not authorize to-day? Is closure to be applied in order that the control of parliament over the treasury of this Dominion shall be ignored and be no longer effective? I want to know where the defenders of parliamentary rights are this afternoon. Where are those who once talked for days and nights about the "rights of parliament," who indeed have so deported themselves in this House that one would be led to believe a government should be not the initiator of legislation but a mere committee to carry out the specified will of parliament as expressed' in resolutions? Where are the defenders of parliamentary rights now? Hon. gentlemen to my left have sat by and voted for the administration while the administration, by devious, indefensible, illegal means, has defeated the will of parliament and defied its rights. Does anyone for a moment suggest that this government had any justification in the world for ignoring the parliament of Canada last session and projecting this Dominion into an enterprise in the district of Rouyn to the extent of $5,000,000?

The Address-Mr. Forke
If so, I should like to ask hon. gentlemen to my left, and hon. gentlemen opposite as well, this question: why did we debate in parliament, not through one session but two, projects precisely similar in character though of far less importance because far less in cost? Why did we debate them in this House, compelling them to run the vicissitudes of the House of Commons and the perils of the Senate, if the government could simply have turned their backs upon us and through orders in council, contrived by clever American lawyers, have devised a means of defying the Commons and Senate both?
The only defence in respect of this flagrant disregard of the rights of parliament comes from him who is all the time preaching that politics must not be dragged into the railways, but who seems to believe that the converse is entirely justifiable, that the railways may at his single will be dragged into politics. Is it to be said that because some lawyer is able to devise a scheme whereby parliament may be ignored, whereby a bond issue or a construction contract can be labelled a lease, then a government guilty of yielding to a proposal of that kind is nevertheless entitled not only to the support of this House but to closure in order that its desires may be gratified? Yet such is the position in which this government finds itself this afternoon. Parliament, at its instance, is voting closure for the purpose of an adjournment; closure for the purpose of giving the House a holiday; closure for the purpose of robbing the most important committee which has sat here for twenty years of all power to do its duty; closure for the purpose of shielding the government from attack on charges of defiance of parliament as grave as ever were laid at the door of any administration. For these purposes closure is invoked this afternoon. The majority will of course impose its rude will over the minority. But this government will pay a penalty not only for its tragic record in the past but for its blunder of today.

I do
not intend to occupy the full twenty minutes which has been allotted to hon. members who wish to speak, but I desire to say a few words in regard to the position which the Progressive party holds in this House. We have sat here patiently listening to long, shall I say sometimes tiresome, speeches-I think I may justly describe them thus-and we have heard a great many things said about the Progressives. We have been told what the Progressives have done, what they have not done, and what
they are likely to do in the future. I must say that I am astonished whenever I hear the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) speaking of co-operation with the Progressives. How can hon. gentlemen expect any co-operation with the group in this part of the House in view of the language which they have used of hon. members in this corner during the past month? Let them read Hansard for that short time and see the terms which hon. gentlemen to my right have applied to the Progressive members during this debate. I will give you a few samples. I listened last night to a wonderful speech from an erudite member representing a cultured constituency in New Ontario.
Let me quote a few sentences from Hansard which he uttered last night:
Their refusal or inability to sit in with the Conservatives was due to what I should term their urban complex, meaning by this a more or less morbid pathological mental process resultant mostly from that diffidence, that timidity, that self-complacency, that parsimony, that narrowness, that simplicity, incident to rusticity.
This is terrible, Mr. Speaker! It is the worst that has ever been said about us. But he is young yet; he will learn better after a while. I read in a newspaper that the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) in his youth drove a team of oxen, and was so close to agriculture that he even used language now and again that would certainly not be considered parliamentary by yourself, Sir. I do not know what we may expect from agriculture when we get a minister of railways in his seat who is imbued with "that narrowness and that simplicity incident to rusticity." I am curious to know what large city in his constituency the hon. member comes from. I must confess I do not know very much about that part of the country, but I should be surprised to learn that there are as yet any very large urban centres there. However, this is by the way. I did not intend to refer to it, but I was asked by hon. friends to my right to give quotations of remarks about the Progressives that had been made' by representative Conservatives.
Now, what is the situation? The members of this House did not create it; the people of Canada created it. I have heard members on both sides blame the third party for the situation which confronted us at the opening of parliament. I may be wrong, but I make the guess that had there been no third party the situation would not have been any better than it is, because I am inclined to believe that two parties would have been so evenly balanced that it would have been very difficult for either to carry on the business of the country. Hon. gentlemen to my right have
The Address-Mr. Forke

spoken as if they had a majority in this House. They have even said that the government had no right to function. Well, if that is so, which party had the right to take office? That is what I should like to know. Hon. members to my right apparently take it for granted that they have a right to form the government. But they have not a majority of this House. What would have happened had the government been defeated? Could the right hon. leader of the opposition have carried on?
No.

We know perfectly well he
could not. He would have had to appeal to the country. Can any member of this House say to-day what would happen if we had a new election?
Yes.

They think they know, but
they do not know. I prophesy to my friends fiom the province of Manitoba that they will never have seven Conservatives from that province within a generation.
Mr. Speaker-
Sit down.

I know the peculiarities of
the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins). If he will come up to my room after a while I will try to convince him that I am right.
Does the hon. gentleman remember-
Sit down.
Does the hon. gentleman remember-
Order.
Order. I understand the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) allows the question that the right hon. gentleman is trying to put?
Oh, yes.

I am asking the hon.
member if he recalls his prophecies in the last parliament?

I admit, Mr. Speaker, that
it is very foolish to prophesy. But I am not discouraged. I would turn to hon. gentlemen opposite and prophesy, too, that there are not going to be very many Liberals from Manitoba after the next election. But there are going to be a great many more Progressives. While I am in the prophesying mood I will go a little further: After another election we are going to see this corner of the

House filled up with just as many Progressives as were returned to the last parliament.
Oh, oh.

My friends may laugh, but
I ask them to remember when that time comes what I am now saying. When we came to this parliament we found no party had a majority in the House of Commons over all other parties. Consequently the first thing we had to do was to find out which party was likely to be able to secure a majority of the members. We voted first of all upon the question:	Had the government a right to
call parliament together? The government was sustained in that division. The position taken by the Progressives was largely influenced by the legislation we are interested in. We have heard "bribery" mentioned by the right hon. leader of the opposition. He has used that word again and again. It is an ugly word, and I do not like it at all. Bribery has never been practised in this House so far as we are concerned. Can any member on either side of the House assert that I know anything about bribes? I defy any member to make such a statement. A legislative programme has been set forth by the government. Surely we have common sense and good judgment enough, notwithstanding our "rusticity", to understand just exactly what that means. We believe it is a programme in the interests not only of our own constituencies but of the whole Dominion. So why call it "bribery" because we accept that programme? The right hon. leader of the opposition talks about co-operation. I wonder if he would not have been willing at the commencement of the session to co-operate with the Progressives if he could have done so. I would not blame him. It would have been all right on his part and quite honourable. Then why throw innuendoes across the floor at those who have co-operated? Why blame them? I think what was done was perfectly honourable on all sides. We have decided to support the government in their legislative programme, and shall do so until that programme is put through.
Now, we have heard a good deal about the government defying the will of parliament. I say the government has not defied the will of parliament. Parliament can defeat this or any other government any day it likes, and once parliament has made up its mind against the government it can no longer remain in office. Then why all this talk during the past six weeks about the government defying the will of the people? We have heard somewhat similar criticism of the Progressives for the course they have taken this session. I

The Address-Mr. Rogers
want to tell hon. gentlemen, no matter on which side of the House they sit, that when they talk in that strain, they are not insulting members of the Progressive group, they are insulting the constituencies that sent those members down here. Those constituencies have confidence in the members they elected to this House. I believe that every action we have taken this session is perfectly legitimate and perfectly honourable, and I hope that what we have done will enure to the benefit of the whole Dominion.

Mr. Speaker, seldom if ever in the history of parliamentary government in Canada has any parliament been called upon to meet conditions similar to those which have confronted this parliament from the first day of the session diown to the present time. These conditions make it abundantly clear that this so-called government has so far not been able to function as a responsible government. Let me say further that this government cannot function as a responsible government in the future, and never can function as a government capable of administering the public affairs of the Dominion of Canada.
Hon. gentlemen opposite two weeks ago realized, probably as no government has ever realized before, the imperative necessity of finding in some form or other a plan which would save them from complete ruin. Of one thing they were certain; of one thing they were sure, that a vote of want of confidence they could not and dare not attempt to face. Something had to be done and that something had to be done quickly. At a given moment all eyes on the other side of the chamber were focussed on the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird), who quickly rose in his place and fulfilled the fondest hope of hon. gentlemen opposite by moving the previous question, thereby extending the stricken, helpless and hopeless condition of hon. gentlemen opposite for two or three weeks longer. I say further that the government, as indicated by their course yesterday and today, still feel the strain of their position, and how could it be otherwise? This much comfort they apparently take to-day, that when the motion came before this House last night it synchronized entirely with what is commonly discussed in this parliament as the fifty-day clause, through which indemnities of $4,000 a year have been made safe for hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House.
Order.

There is nothing out of order. Now, Mr. Speaker, the fifty days
were uip and we had the motion as presented to-day by my hon. friend who leads the House (Mr. Lapointe). My hon. friend has been talking about obstruction, and I want to say here and now that my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) and those around him on this side of the House have never undertaken to obstruct hon. gentlemen opposite. Let me say further that if we had wanted to obstruct it would have been impossible to do so, by reason of the fact that there was nothing before the House to obstruct. Hon. gentlemen opposite could not and dared not bring any measure before this parliament for consideration.
How could we do it until the Address was passed?

Is that all my hon. friend knows of the rules of parliament? Let me point out to my hon. friend what he could do. He certainly is very lacking in knowledge of parliamentary procedure. The day the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne came to this House, my hon. friend's leader rose in his place and made a motion, as follows:	[DOT]
Hon. Ernest Lapointe (Leader of the House): I move, seconded by Mr. Macdonald (Antigonish-Guysborough)
Seconded by my hon. friend.
-that the Speech of His Excellency the Governor General to both Houses of parliament be taken into consideration on Monday next, and that this order have precedence over all other business of the House except government notices of motion and introduction of bills, until disposd of.
Now Mr. Speaker, hon. gentlemen on this side took no objection to that; we wanted to proceed with the business. There are many motions promised in the Speech from the Throne-government notices of motion-
You agreed to that resolution.
Of course we agreed to it.
No other business could come before the House until the Address was disposed of.

With the exception of government notices of motion. Where was the notice of motion in respect to the Hudson Bay railway? Why was that not brought down for consideration? This House was here for business.
We will bring it down.

Why did the government
not bring down a notice of motion in respect to rural credits, which is a very important
The Address-Mr. Rogers

matter? Why was not a notice of motion brought down in respect to a commission to be appointed to inquire into Maritime rights, in my hon. friend's own province? Why was that motion not before the House?
The notice is on the order paper; iet it stay there.
That is what the hon. gentleman wants; he is afraid to bring it before the House.

My hon. friend will see whether we
are afraid, when we get this House started.

My hon. friend acts that
way.
Order.

Now, Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House are quite prepared to deal with private bills and questions. We have now almost a book with 180 questions and fifty or sixty or seventy resolutions, and we on this side of the House are prepared to consent at any time to go on with those matters and get them out of the way. But hon. gentlemen opposite have not, since the opening day, dared to take the opportunity of bringing any measure before this House. That is the trouble with hon. gentlemen opposite; we have been here for nearly two months and not one item of business 'has been brought down.
My hon. friend the leader of the government spoke about this question of adjourning and he said that we on this side of the House had obstructed by speaking too long on the Address. I would like to know, Mr. Speaker, what else we were to do in order to grasp the opportunity which we had of exposing to the intelligent people of this country the weaknesses and the helplessness of hon. gentlemen opposite. Notwithstanding that, we were prepared at any moment and at any time to take up any business brought before us. The fact that we have been carrying on in addressing this House for some time means no additional expense to the country, whether we continued to expose the conditions whicn we met here, or whether we were prepared to support an adjournment.
Still more amazing, Mr. Speaker, was the statement of my hon. friend who leads this House to-day in coupling the present closure with the closure brought in by the Conservative party in 1913. I want to point out to this House, and particularly to my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Macdonald)-who I am sorry to see has left the

chamber because he needs a little light on some of these important questions-the difference between the situation that existed then and that which confronts us to-day. Some one has argued that the closure measure of a few years ago was the reason why we had a closure motion before parliament to-day. But, Mr. Speaker, to mention the closure of that time in comparison with the closure measure of to-day is nothing short of an insult to the intelligence of the Canadian people. Who is there in Canada that does not know that unpreparedness for war cost Canada untold millions in treasure and many thousands of priceless lives? The Conservative party believed in 1913 that there was danger, and serious danger, and hence our naval proposals were brought before parliament. We were met with the argument that our naval proposals were submitted to the House under false pretences, that we had put in the mouth of His Royal Highness the Governor General assertions that were absolutely unfounded in fact, when we placed in the Speech from the Throne the assertion that a condition of things existed in Great Britain which made it imperative that the naval forces of the empire should at once be strengthened. On this line of argument parliament was kept in session for days and months until the government were finally obliged to bring down a closure measure. Unfortunately for Canada, the Liberal Senate defeated our naval proposals, and for so doing Liberal senators and the Liberal party in Canada received the applause of the enemies of Great Britain and her dominions. I should like to support that statement by an extract from one of the leading papers in Germany, which, dealing with our proposals at that time, said:
Whatever may be decided upon later, the actual decision of the Canadian Senate means at any rate a heavy moral and material loss for the defence of the empire, for Mr. Borden's promise has been foolishly enough counted on. His offer made an enormous impression on the whole world. Mr. Churchill pointed out this fact, especially in the well-known memorandum of the admiralty. This impression will not only be destroyed, but people will everywhere obtain the conviction that England cannot depend on such help from her colonies. "By rivals and enemies," says the Morning Post today, "the decision will be eagerly welcomed. By friends it will be regarded as ominous." The impression must inevitably be created that the solidarity of the empire is a myth, and that those powers which would like to see the overthrow of British naval supremacy need not be discouraged in their efforts by the thought that their challenge would be met by the united resources of the Mother Country and of every one of the daughter states.-
Those were the conditions, Mr. Speaker, under which we brought down our naval proposals to parliament, and in connection with which closure was introduced, and no one

The Address-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
will say that those conditions are at all comparable with the conditions to-day.
Before I conclude, I want to address a word or two to my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke), who was good enough to speak of conditions in the province of Manitoba, from which I come. I want to tell the hon. member for Brandon that as long 5 p.m. as he lives he will never again sit for a constituency in the province of Manitoba in this parliament of Canada. Notwithstanding the combined support that he had in the last election, with the Liberal party united with the so-called Progressive party, his majority under those conditions was rather limited, and it will be entirely wiped out upon the next occasion.
Let me bring to the attention of the House a statement made by the Prime Minister in respect to his majority in the last House, and I bring this forward simply because it accounts to some extent for the atmosphere that is to be found in certain quarters of this parliament. The Prime Minister is reported as follows:
"If I went out for dinner, mjr majority of one was gone." When he formed his administration, however, he felt he would get sufficient assistance from the other side of the House to enable him to carry on. There is an indemnity of $4,000 and 'he thought the Progressives would think twice before they voted against it.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know what the Prime Minister had in his mind when he said that, but he said something more. The question was asked him:
What about the Progressives helping you?
And Mr. King replied:
Let me answer that clearly. When the Progressives take the attitude that they will support us when we do what they want, and we can go to blazes when we do not, you cannot get very .far that way. You cannot get anything done in parliament under those conditions.
Now let me read something that my hon. friend from Brandon had to say in respect to the Prime Minister. Speaking in the city of Regina on September 7, 1925, lie said:
The Prime Minister Mr. Mackenzie King, is urging the western provinces to send to parliament numerous representatives as members of his party caucus on the ground that that would be the best method of obtaining the necessary changes in government policy. This proposal Is an invitation to keep his party in office, and in return to receive such reforms as the party caucus may concede. The irrefutable answer to his plea is written in the record of his party, whose recurring failures to redeem his election promises and to implement his political platforms are matters of public record.
Just one more reference, and this is a statement made by the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King, who, speaking at Moose Jaw on September 30, said:
(The Progressives had an opportunity to elect a government in 1921, but in 1925 they had no such chance. Consequently there was no reason for waste of votes on them. Why waste time and effort on a party that can't form an administration? Mr. Crerar admitted the Progressives could be only a sectional party. Other leaders were abandoning them. The light of Mr. Forke was the flickering torch of Liberalism. All the influence he wielded came from association with other parties in the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, the flickering light of the torch of the hon. member for Brandon has grown strong in the interests of the Liberal party in this parliament. He is as Certain to vote Liberal as my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough; he is quite as safe, quite as sure; he always has been, and always will be. But that is his business, and not ours. I simply want this parliament to know the facts and to understand the conditions. The information may be helpful to hon. gentlemen opposite, and I hope they will take full advantage of it.
I am told my time is up. In conclusion, let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the time is not far distant when we shall find hon. gentlemen opposite in the position to which they were relegated by the electors of this Dominion on the 29th of October last.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, twenty minutes
is not a very long period in which to make a defence, if defence were needed-and I do not think any defence is required-of the action of the government in calling parliament and the steps it has taken since that date. One could not help being interested in the debate that was being carried on in this House although a great deal of it consisted of severe criticism of the government of to-day, criticism that was unwarranted, in my opinion, and that at times descended to what I would call back-door or baek-yard_ discussion, rather than that of gentlemen in this House of Commons. Let me rehearse very briefly why parliament was summoned. The leader of the House (Mr. Lapointe) gave us a resume this afternoon of the reasons for convening parliament. We are warranted in taking the position we do with respect to closure on this occasion. We are warranted in sustaining parliament when parliament decided by a majority vote in this House that a certain procedure should be taken. That is our answer to the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) as to why at this moment closure is applied. It is applied because they and their followers have been attempting to defy the will of parliament dearly expressed.

As I have barely twenty minutes in which to address the House I shall not endeavour to cover completely the speech of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), but there are a couple of points in that speech to which I should like to refer for a moment if I may.
In the first place the minister, in regard to the Rouyn railway, suggested that we could investigate the matter in this House or in a committee of the House. I submit however that as this railway was incorporated as a private concern in the province of Quebec
we can do nothing of the sort. A fact that has often struck me is this, that invariably in this House, the shadier the deal the more certain is it that my hon. friend will be put up to defend it. As I said last year, the hon. gentleman looks more respectable than anyone could possibly be in real life; he fairly oozes respectability. Whenever therefore there is a Shady deal of any kind to be defended he is always put up on his feet to defend it.
I want to touch one other point mentioned by the minister, and that is in regard to taxation. He said that this government had reduced taxation to a considerable extent. Well, in the first place it has not done so; but even if it had reduced taxation it has cut down business ten times more than it *has effected such reduction.
Sir, we have had in the last few hours the amazing and amusing spectacle of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who has been described by his admirers and his followers as the tribune of the people, the apostle of 'Liberalism, the defender of free speech, rising in his place and clamping closure on the debate which has been going on, notwithstanding that this procedure has been condemned not only by him, as my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) has pointed out, but by most hon. gentlemen opposite, as an infamous gag, an instrument of autocracy, gag law, and generally as the quintessence of Tory autocracy. Yet, as I watched the vote being taken, the only hon. gentleman who had the decency to blush, as supporters of the government one after another swallowed themselves once more, was my hon. hiend the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon), a gentleman who probably blushes as little as any hon. member in this House.
This act of closure is, Mr. Speaker, the culminating act of a series of humiliating retractions, of flagrant violations of promises, and of a wholesale swallowing of so-called Liberal principles on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite. I remember that as a boy I once went to a circus where I saw the performance of a sword swallower, but the ability of that man to swallow swords was nothing compared to the ability of this government to swallow its principles and its promises. The government has long since cast aside practically every one of its professed principles, just as it has broken all its promises; and now this last flimsy principle among all the principles of Liberalism, namely, the principle of free speech, of which hon. gentlemen opposite have spoken so much, the government has sacrificed on the same altar
The Address-Mr. Manion

at which they are all worshipping to-day, the altar of power at any price, even the price of Canada itself.
We have had for four years the spectacle of a government recanting all its promises and its principles. Let me mention a few of these recantations. The tariff plank of 1919 is burned; Senate reform, of which hon. gentlemen opposite have spoken so much from one end of Canada to the other, is forgotten; national economy, of which they have made a great boast, has been replaced by the political pork barrel; trusts, combines and mergers, of which Mr. Mackenzie King and Mr. Murdock talked so much, are merely given a new title,-they are now called monopolies by land and sea; the cost of living, over which Mr. Mackenzie King has literally fumed for the past seven or eig!ht years, has gone up instead of down; free speech is now wiped out by closure; and national unity is eliminated, sacrificed on the same altar. Why, speaking of national unity, it seems to me almost a sacrilege for some of my hon. friends opposite, although by no means all of them, to use this phrase at all after the very wicked and vile methods which were adopted in the province of Quebec by some of them in the last election, methods which showed that they were more anxious to defeat my right hon. leader than they were to advocate such policies and defend such principles as they knew were vital to the prosperity of the people of that province. And the result of these various recantations to which I have alluded has been that we have had serious business depression in this country, marked unemployment, and an appalling exodus of our population such as we have never before experienced in the history of Canada. So much are these facts recognized by the people of the Dominion that on October 29 the government was overwhelmingly defeated, the Prime Minister and eight of his ministers being completely rejected. The Liberal party had 200,000 votes less than this party, and to-day in this House they have fifteen members fewer than we have on this side. At the present time four provinces in this great Dominion are without representation in the cabinet, and we have the humiliating spectacle of the province of Ontario, the greatest province in Canada both in point of wealth and in the matter of population, without a single minister in the government, while the little province of Saskatchewan has a representation of three. Yet the Minister of Justice declared a few minutes ago that we were obstructing parliament. Why, Mr. Speaker, the government has been guilty of a far more serious

obstruction than the obstruction of parliament, even if that charge were true in respect of this party: the government has obstructed the will of the people. That is what my hon. friends opposite have done. We have obstructed, it is true, but, we have obstructed not any business of parliament-there has been no business before parliament to be obstructed-but the efforts of the government to vote itself a holiday.
What was the reply of the people on October 29 to the Speech which had been delivered by the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King at Richmond Hill, in which, for a few brief moments, he played the part of a sportsman, when he declared that he would not come back to parliament and attempt to carry on unless he was in a better position from a parliamentary standpoint than he had been in the past to implement the promises he had made the country? What was the reply of the people to that speech? Their reply was to wipe out altogether not only the Prime Minister himself but his ministers in the province of Ontario and in various other parts of the country as well. Yet to-day, in face of this unequivocal verdict of the people on October 29, Mr. Mackenzie King says that he is going to carry through a great deal of legislation forecast in the Speech from the Throne,-a Speech which, by the way, ought never to have been introduced at all if the government had been really sincere in its announcement that parliament would meet merely for the purpose of ascertaining what party should govern.
Mr. Mackenzie King had in the last parliament, between 1921 and 1925, 80 per cent of the members of the House of Commons, including the sixty-five Progressives who voted in support of the government on every vital occasion. What is the situation to-day? To-day he has, including the three or four groups outside the Conservatives, only 53 per cent of the membership. And yet, although in the last parliament, with such support as I have indicated, he found it impossible to go on with the Hudson Bay railway, to give Alberta her resources, to bring in rural credits, to enact the single transferable vote, or to carry out one single promise of all the multitude of promises he had made to every section of the country, to-day he declares his intention of undertaking all or most of these things. If he could not fulfil any of these promises or institute any of these policies with 80 per cent of the membership of this House, how on earth is he going to do so with 53 per cent of the members? If he could not carry on with majorities ranging from 77 to 116 between 1921 and 1925, figures which I

The Address-Mr. Manion
have taken the trouble to verify, how will he carry on with majorities of from 1 to 10 as they have had this session? That very fact, Mr. Speaker, that his majorities to-day range between 1 and 10, is the most outstanding proof that we were absolutely right in saying that he and his party were indisputably defeated in the country on October 29.
The present situation would be a laughable and hilarious farce were it not so tragical from the standpoint of the people of this Dominion. Notwithstanding all this, however, the hon. member for Brandon gets up in this House and votes for closure in order to keep this ragged remnant of a government in power, this alleged government which since coming into office has broken every promise it ever made to western Canada itself. My hon. friend (Mr. Forke) is apparently still willing and happy to accept that same useless coin, that same gold brick which he got from Mr. Mackenzie King in the past. In other words, Sir, his political partisanship is so strong that he prefers to see Mr. Mackenzie King in power rather than see the policies carried out which he stands for in the west. His independence, Mr. Speaker, is only a mask, and everybody knows it is only a mask, just as they know that Mr. Mackenzie King has been the greatest failure as a political leader that this country has ever produced; just as they know that he has been the greatest master of political dodgery in the history of the Dominion, so much so that to-day, instead of being spoken of in many circles as the leader of the Liberal party, he is spoken of as its misleader.
Now, what are the purposes of this closure motion that the hon. member for Brandon so loyally supported a little while ago. It is true we put on closure in the past on important questions such as the naval policy of the Dominion, the Canadian Northern railway purchase, and the railway incorporation. But those were all important questions. What are the purposes, I ask again, of this closure motion? They were mentioned by my leader, but I shall enumerate them again. The first is a desire for a holiday-that the members of this government may go home and laugh in peace and quiet at the country which they are betraying instead of serving. The other purpose is to close up the customs investigation, which of course will help all the lawbreakers, the smugglers, the thugs and the thieves to join them in their laugh at the expense of the people. And yet my hon. friend from Brandon stands up and trails along behind them with a large portion of his group. By his attitude he aids and abet3
those purposes, in fact, to use a term current among lawyers, he is an accomplice before the fact in this case.
We also are tired of the debate; we are tired of the way in which things have been dragging along while we have been trying to spur this government into action, but we felt it a duty we owed to the committee appointed by this House to keep members sitting here in order that we might at least give them moral support in their investigation of the charges made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) who is endeavouring honourably and honestly to save tens of millions of dollars that the people are now being robbed of by those who are breaking our customs laws.
I well remember, Sir, a book I read many years ago by Victor Hugo, in which he describes a man whose cheeks when a boy had been slit by some human monster so that the poor fellow appeared always to be grinning from ear to ear, and he was exhibited throughout Europe as the "laughing man." Well, to my mind this is nothing more than a laughing government. We have had the House sitting for almost two months with the members on this side, as my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior said, telling the government their faults and their failures in every accent from every section of the country. What have we had in reply? Nothing but laughter. Certainly no defence because there is none; our accusations are true. This attitude of laughing instead of acting is in keeping with the whole record of the government for the past four years or more. Why do I say that, Mr. Speaker? Because they have laughed at everything worth while that has been proposed. They laughed first at the promises of Mr. Mackenzie King, their own leader-they laughed at the platform of 1919; then they laughed at the people for allowing themselves to be duped by that platform and the promises of Mr. Mackenzie Ring; they laughed at the appalling unemployment of our Canadian working people; they laughed at the appalling exodus of our Canadian-born; they laughed at a real Canadian policy of "Canada for Canadians" which we tried to persuade them to adopt; they laughed at our proposal to inaugurate a national fuel policy-to use Canadian coal on Canadian railways, and Canadian coal in Canadian homes; they laughed at our policy of using Canadian-made products rather than imported goods; they laughed at all our great national problems instead of trying to solve them; and finally, Mr. Speaker, they have been laughing at the people of Canada ever since October 29, when the electorate

gave a verdict against them, which verdict they have been ever since ignoring instead of accepting.

They are going to get a temporary or permanent respite because, I repeat, the Customs committee cannot deal effectively with any recalcitrant witnesses unless they have at least the moral support of the House.
But I want to remind the government of the old saying-those who laugh last laugh best. And the people are going to have a last laugh, because ultimately they are going to rid themselves for all time of this odious government; they are going to send Mr. Mackenzie King and the member for Brandon-as mentioned by the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) a moment ago-and a number of their friends to that place where weeping and wailing^ and gnashing of teeth prevails instead of laughter. Sir, at one time in the English House of Commons a leader was impeached if he took a vicious or disloyal attitude that was detrimental to the country, which he was supposed to serve. I think the last impeachment took place about a hundred and fifty years ago. It seems to me it is quite possible we may have to re-establish that old practice in Canada, should it be the only way open to us to get rid of a Prime Minister whose mind is impervious to any realization of defeat and whose character is impervious to any appreciation of fair play and sportsmanship-a man who is so impervious to this quality that he is to-day retaining the reins of power long after the people have shown him that they recognize the failure he is, long after they have shown him that they no longer retain any confidence in him.
Closure at this time and under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, simply adds another to the long list of charges against this make-

shift of a government, and it is going to be only another reason why the people will amply revenge themselves when the time comes against an administration which has been such a failure in grappling with the great national questions that urgently demand attention. Mr. King and some of his political accomplices will be sent to the political wilderness directly the people get an opportunity. That opportunity will come shortly, and when it does come, the people will correct the error they made during the last election under the impression that the province of Quebec was voting on the issues of the day.
