there myself before long to help my party. I hope so. The people wild try to correct the error they made in thinking the province of Quebec was voting on the issues of the day instead of against an old conscription law that has long been dbsolete, and against an imaginary Turkish war. My hon. friend speaks of Regina. Well, I notice that the Prime Minister goes to Prince Albert; he does not dare open a constituency nearer home. This great province of Ontario, as large in area and as important in population and resources as any ,other three, ot probably four, provinces, with ;the exception of the province of Quebec, is to-day in the disgraceful position, from the Standpoint of the government, of having no representative in the cabinet. The Prime Minister goes to Saskatchewan to get a seat, ibut he did not dare open any in the province ,of Ontario. When the next election comes, no matter what happens in the province of Quebec-and what I have said of that great province is not in derogation of it, for I have the greatest respect for its people, but I have .little respect for some of the Liberal leaders ,who have misled them-I say, that in the next election, no matter what way the people of Quebec vote, their fellow-citizens throughout the rest of the Dominion are going to raise up such a hurricane of indignation against this government as will sweep out Mr. Mackenzie King, the member for Brandon and his other supporters and sweep into power the Liberal-Conservative party.
Oh, oh.

I hear one of my hon
friends laughing somewhat loudly at that. I do not wish to be offensive, but there was a poet some time ago who referred to "The loud laugh that spoke the vacant mind." I say that, I repeat, with no desire to be offen-

The Address-Mr. Bcaubien
sive in any way. I repeat that the electors are going to put into power the Liberal-Conservative party, standing for a stable tariff policy for all the people of this country; for p sane, economical railway policy; for a lower taxation policy and for a progressive immigration policy in Canada. Those policies are the foundation stones upon which the greatness of Canada must be built, and they must be held together by the cement of fair dealing between the different sections of Canada. .The country knows that this government will not put those policies into effect; the country knows also that those policies are absolutely necessary. With the exception of the government itself, everyone knows that this is what we must have in order that we may join up with those advancing, progressive and prosperous nations in other parts of the world.
In rising to make a few remarks on this occasion, Mr. Speaker, I do so with the view of justifying my actions in this House during this session of parliament.
It cannot be done.

Possibly not in the eyes of some people, but it can in the eyes of the electors whom I have the honour to represent.
I am not concerned with what the Liberals said) against or in favour of the closure; I am concerned with the conditions as they exist to-day, and I say that if the electors of this country are going to be subjected to obstruction in this House for weeks and weeks, consisting largely of reiteration of what happened during the campaign, of what the political leaders said or did not say during the campaign, or what they said that they should not have said, I am afraid1 the electors will lose confidence in our parliamentary institutions.	.
What is the duty of a member? The first duty of a member is to his electors, in my opinion. When we came down here no party had an absolute majority over the others, and we had to consider what course we should follow; we had to form a plan of action in order to be true to the principles upon which we were elected. I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, the principles upon which I was elected. I was elected to come down here to force the two parties which have existed since confederation to put their promises into effect. I happened to be in Montreal two or three weeks ago, and while there a man said to me, "What do you wild westerners want?" To which I replied: "We want what both political parties have been promising us for the last twenty-five years." Is it too much to expect?
That is what I ask. The Hudson Bay railway ; rural credits; the return of their natural resources to the western provinces-those are all in the Speech from the Throne, and those are the promises made by both political parties for years, on public platforms, in this House and everywhere else.
We came down here and the government presented His Excellency's Speech. The return of the natural resources to Alberta was mentioned in that Speech; the completion of the Hudson Bay railway was mentioned, as well as the question of rural credits. What is left for us to do? I am not partial; I am not here to defend the Liberal party or praise the Conservative party; I am here to defend my actions and I can defend them before my electors.
What was there to do? The Speech from the Throne was drafted by the government, because it was presented by the government. The Speech from the Throne was acceptable to the Progressives and they voted against the amendment of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen). The Independent members also accepted the Speech from the Throne in voting against that amendment. The right hon. leader of the opposition accepted the Speech from the Throne, because in moving his amendment he used the words "that the following be added," and my understanding is that when you add anything you accept what is already there. My knowledge of English may be limited, but that is my understanding of the word "add" and I do not think anyone who understands the English language can take any other meaning from it. Then, if the government accepts the Speech from the Throne; if we accept it and the leader of the opposition accepts it, what is there for us to do? Have we done anything wrong? Where is the bribe? I have not seen any bribe, and I do not know of any. I have acted according to my conscience and according to the expressed desire of my electors. That has been my only ambition in this House and will be my only ambition as long as I have the honour to represent a constituency in this parliament.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I said some two years ago, and I repeated it in this present parliament, that the speeches should be curtailed to the shortest possible time. I am rather glad to see this closure; I would like to see closure applied quite often when there is obstruction, and I think the government would be justified-if they are going to be a government-in showing some backbone and saying, "We are here with certain measures which we have mentioned in the Speech from the

The Address-Mr. Beaubien
Throne, and' the moment obstruction looms up we are going to put on the closure." That is the stand I would take, whether the right hon. leader of the opposition headed the government, or whether the present government remained in power. The people expect results, and not wind; three, four and five hour^ speeches are going to cause people to be disgusted with the members of parliament and with our parliamentary institutions.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is just one remark the horn, member for Rainy River made which X think he will correct at the first opportunity. He said that the Progressives voted with the government during the last parliament and during the last session. I want to 'be fair, and I am sure that if the hon. member will look up the records he will find that he and his party voted with the Liberals to defeat the Progressives oftener than we voted with the Liberals.

Will my hon. friend permit me an interruption? The hon. gentleman forgets that I said "on all vital matters." And may I add, just in a word, on all matters where there was any doubt of the government carrying the vote.

I will leave it at that, and I say again that the Conservatives voted oftener with the Liberals than the Progressives did. I mention this because I am sure the hon. member for Rainy River wants to be fair, as he is always fair.

Will the hon. member
permit an interruption? The hon. member designates the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) as the member for Rainy River, and the hon. member for Fort William evidently desires to be the member for Rainy River, and accepts that designation. I would just like to correct that error.

I am very glad of the
correction.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon.

I am sorry. The hon.
member CMr. Manion) represented Rainy River last year, which was the reason for my error. It is a good thing to change a constituency sometimes.
Now Mr. Speaker, I do not want to delay the House any longer. In closing I appeal to the government and to every member of this House: when the House meets again on March 15, let us have a programme.

Hear, hear.

'Mr. BEAUBIEN: I mean a programme of legislation; let the government present the legislation. I may make a slip in the use ,of a word once in a while; I did not mean that exactly. It does a man good, Mr. Speaker, to see the opposition laugh, because they have been so solemn the last few days that one would think they had a funeral on hand. In fact, the Manitoba Free Press .stated that the committee of strategy of the Conservative party was in distress. I wonder if the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) has received an SjOB. call from them, and whether he has sent relief?
Let us forget our political strife. Let us try to work in harmony, because it is the only way we can get anywhere. If hon. members are going to rehash that old political stuff .across the floor of this House, the country is going to suffer, and the members who are jiere are going to suffer at the next election.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to occupy very much of the time of the House in discussing whether or not the Closure rule should be applied aJt this stage of the debate. I am sure every hon. member realizes that the debate on the Address has already occupied1 an unprecedented time; that every subject possible has been brought to the attention of the House by hon. members who have spoken, and that there is no justification or reason why the House should be further delayed from proceeding at the proper time to take into consideration the government programme and to have it crystallized into legislation.
Hon. gentlemen who spoke this afternoon said that this resolution should not be adopted, first, because it only meant that there was going to be a holiday. It will not be any holiday for the government; we expect that every day between now and the fifteenth instant will be taken up in serious consideration, in meetings of council, of the legislation which we propose to submit immediately after parliament resumes its sittings. That legislation which is stated in the Speech from the Throne will be made ready at the earliest possible day for the consideration of the House.
It has been suggested that the committee which has been working so steadily will have its operations interrupted. I have had a long
MARCH 2, 1926	i
The Address-Mr. Macdonald (Antigonish)
experience in connection with investigating and other committees amd such a suggestion is purely imaginary. If the committee continues to sit as it has been doing during the past weeks, there will be seven days on which it will sit between now and the 15th of March. Up to the present there has been no refusal on the part of any witness to answer questions put by the committee and there is no indication of any such disposition on the part of any witness who has been summoned. My hon. friends know very well that in accordance with the practice that has existed for all time in parliament, the plenary power of parliament to deal with persons who refuse to answer questions extends to detention only during the sitting of the House, so that this theory that the committee is to be hampered in any way is a delusion and a figment of the imagination put forward solely to formulate some excuse for further delaying the business of this country.
My right hon. friend is worried because we have applied to him and his colleagues a weapon which he placed in the rules of the House. Why should we not do so? In 1913 that rule was placed there in the form of an amendment to the rules by my right hon. friend in the midst of a dehate on a certain subject. That amendment to the rules was not made after full consideration of the rules at the proper time, but the government of the day, intervening in the debate which was before the House, framed the rule and had it passed by the majority at that time. It is an accepted situation not only in Canada but in every English-speaking parliamentary body that where obstruction exists or appears in the form in which it appears in this House, that rule should be invoked1 in the public interest in order that the business of the country may be carried on.
I turn my attention to a matter which has been discussed frequently by my colleagues from the Maritime provinces; and for various reasons I want to refer to that question as it has been presented by some of my hon. friends. The matter first came to the attention of the House when the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith) delivered an address early in the debate and quoted what he said was the bill of rights of the Maritime provinces, the first one being:
The restoration of the integrity of .the Intercolonial railway, with the western terminus of the system reestablished at Montreal.
It will be noted that my hon. friend is not very clear in his statement whether or not it is intended that the Intercolonial should be detached altogether from the Canadian National and run by the government as a
separate entity, or whether it Should be run as one of the divisions of the Canadian National Railways. The difference between the two is very important and it is desirable that it should be defined in order that the House may recognize it. I understand my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) is opposed to either of those tilings being done. As a Maritime man I believe the Fathers of Confederation, when they placed in the British North America Act provision for the construction of what was known as the Intercolonial railway, intended that that railway should be operated for all time in regard to both through and local rates in the interest of the Maritime provinces on account of the fact that they were distant from the central part of Canada. I know for fifty years this parliament and public men on both sides of politics have recognized that as being the manner under which that railway should be operated, and it was so operated until 1918. I have under my hand the order in council, passed on the 20th November, 1918, which took that railway away from the position which it then occupied, by which they removed Mr. Hays and Mr. Brady, who were general managers respectively of the eastern and western lines and the order proceeds:
Ami His Excellency the Governor General in Council, is further pleased to order and declare that the persons, from time to time comprising the Board of Directors of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, shall be and they are hereby appointed a Board of Management of the Canadian Government railways, and are hereby given the powers vested in the General Manager under the general regulations of the Canadian Government Railways adopted by order in Council of the 22nd January, 1914, (P.G. 184).
Mr. Hanna came in and took charge of the railways, and by a subsequent order in December the name of the company was changed and these directors were styled the Canadian National Railway directors. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Cantley) became one of the directors of the railway in conjunction with Mr. Hanna, and my hon. friend from Pictou and Mr. Hanna brought into effect these railway rates which have been in existence, with some amendments, since that date. All these rates in force on the Canadian Government railways to-day, so far as they apply to the Maritime provinces, were brought into effect when my hon. friend for Pictou was one of the directors of the company. In order that *there might be no doubt about that, I wired to Mr. Dalrymple, the chief traffic manager and vice president of the Canadian National, and this is what he said:
Many changes have been made in downward direction in Maritime rates since 1921 including building material,
J456	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Macdonald (Antigonish)
iron and steel articles, lumber, potatoes, grain and grain products and fertilizers. Rates between Prince Edward Island and mainland have been placed on main line basis; export and import via Halifax placed on St. John basis; reductions in class rates between Maritimes and points west of Montreal.
Those have been made since Mr. Hanna retired and since my hon. friend retired as one of the directors of the company, and since Sir Henry Thornton came in. I did not hear my hon. friend from Pictou, or any of those gentlemen previous to 1921 raising their voices in objection to the system of rates. We hear it now. At the instance of this government at the present time an investigation is going on for the purpose of ascertaining whether or not the discriminatory rates should be removed!. [DOT] For the information of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Quinn), let me state that when his party were in power down to 1921 there was discrimination against St. John and' Halifax in favour of American ports in regard to grain passing through Canada. That discrimination was removed two years ago by Sir Henry Thornton, and to-day grain can be carried to Halifax and St. John, although it is a longer distance, at exactly the same rates as to Portland and Boston. That objection has been removed. Last year objection was made to the construction of proper elevator facilities.
Before the hon. gentleman leaves the Intercolonial-
I object to interruptions. I have only twenty minutes to speak.
I would like to say-
Sit down.
Order, order.

I am mentioning these facts to show the House that I agree that there are matters to be investigated and considered, but in regard to the question of coal duty I desire to remind my hon. friend that the miners of Cape Breton have passed a resolution objecting to any increase in the coal duties.

When?
Mr. MACDONALD' (Antigonish-Guysbor-ough): Two or three months ago.
Have you a copy of the resolution?
No. My hon. friend knows it was passed just before the beginning of the negotiations with the Besco Company.
I would like to see a copy of the resolution. .

I can get it for my hon. friend. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis (Mr. Short) addressed the House on the subject of the fisheries down there. I sympathize with him in full in regard to all those matters he mentioned. I think that industry deserves the greatest possible encouragement from all parts of Canada, but it is rather difficult for the government to make people eat fish if they do not want to. However, we are ready to do anything in our power to assist in the transportation of fish and the development of that industry. But let me call attention to a resolution which was passed in the provincial legislature, moved by the Conservative leader, Mr. Corning, on April 23, 1923. I would like to put this resolution on Hansard1. I quote a portion of it:
Whereas, the spirit of the confederation compact with respect to the Intercolonial Railway, now a part of the Canadian National Railway system, has been violated and Nova Scotia as a province of Canada is not receiving fair and equitable treatment with respect to freight rates, railway, shipping and other matters on which the province's economic development depends.
And whereas, handicapped by high freight rates and our remoteness from the populous centres of Canada, Nova Scotia cannot compete in Ontario and Quebec with the farm or forest products of those provinces.
And whereas, the markets of Nova Scotia are now being invaded with the surplus farm, dairy, orchard and industrial products of Ontario, Quebec and other provinces which offer no reciprocal markets for the similar products of this province.
And whereas, Nova Scotia as a part of Canada is supporting the policy and practice of heavy protective duties, mainly foT the advantage and benefit of the manufacturing and farming communities of Ontario and Quebec thereby increasing the cost of living in this province without any commensurate benefit to our people.
And whereas. Ontario, Quebec and the western provinces are indifferent to the development and use of the Canadian Atlantic ports, and the policy of the Canadian National Railway is diverting Canadian commerce and shipping traffic through foreign ports to the detriment and injury of the Canadian Atlantic ports and at the sacrifice of Canadian economic independence.
And whereas, confederation has hindered the natural development of this province, impairing its markets at home and abroad and compelling increasing thousands of its most thrifty citizens to emigrate to other lands.
And whereas, the burden of taxation, federal and provincial, has become intolerable to the people of Nova Scotia who have to bear their full share of heavy tariff duties and the loss from the operation of huge railway systems, which railways are building up the commerce of American ports at the expense of the Canadian Atlantic ports and the Intercolonial Railway.
And whereas, Nova Scotia if an independent, selfgoverning British dominion, would be able to protect its farmers, fishermen and industrial workers through tariff measures and trade treaties, thus preserving its home market and furnishing employment

The Address-Mr. Macdonald (Antigonish)
to its people and profitable investment for capital and build up the enterprise and population of this province,
Therefore resolved, that in the opinion of this House a vote of the electors of Nova Scotia should be taken by way of referendum for the purpose of ascertaining whether the people of this province favour its withdrawal from confederation and the reconstitution of Nova Scotia as an independent, self-governing British dominion.
That was the Conservative policy in Nova Scotia in 1923. The resolution in amendment moved by the then leader of the government set out the policy of the provincial government, on that subject.
You drove them to it.

Where is he now?
1458	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Macdonald (Antigonish)

He is in the
Liberal party.

In a manifesto issued some time ago
he said:
And first let me speak of the so-called national policy or system of protection, under and by virtue of which it is certainly true that the manufacturers of Ontario and Quebec have fatten fd and grown rich, even although they are now passing through a lean period.
We who live in Nova Scotia must pay the tribute to Ontario and Quebec exacted by the so-called national policy, but when we come to a question of protecting our interests and our ports, that we are told is another matter.
And he goes further and says in a letter:
The present customs tariff of Canada protects principally the manufacturers of central provinces who, taking advantage of it, raised their prices to the point that the cost of living of our people and the production costs of our natural industries are so great that our producers cannot compete successfully in foreign markets with the producers of other countries where living and production costs are lower.
That is the statement and the position-taken toy the Hon. Mr. McCurdy.
He is not a Conservative.

You had better go and tell him
that. Then again he reiterates on another page:
We believe that the policy of protection as applied to Nova Scotia to-day constitutes a burden which is crushing us.
That is the position taken by Mr. Mc-McCurdy. Mr. McCurdy has a right to his opinion, just as much as my hon. friends. He has a right to express his views in regard to these matters, and his views differ somewhat from those expressed by my hon. friends. It seems to me that the attitude of the government that a commission be appointed in order to arrive at just what the difficulty in the Maritime provinces is, is -a reasonable one. My hon. friend from Labdlle (Mr. Bourassa) made the suggestion that the matter might be inquired into by a committee of the House. That is well worthy of consideration. But here we have these varying and different views as to the real situation and the cause of it. On the one hand hon. members want more duty. On the other hand one of their confreres in the legislature of Nova .Scotia declared quite two years ago that protection was injuring the Maritime provinces, ,and moved a resolution that a plebiscite should be taken to ascertain the feeling in that province.
Did you not ask for duties on coal and steel?

My hon. friend knows that I have a record of which I am not ashamed, and I am here to say that as a Nova Scotian and a Maritime man I stand firmly for everything that will make for the progress and the prosperity of that part of the Dominion. In my judgment, the intention of the Fathers of Confederation in regard to the Intercolonial railway should be clearly recognized and carried into effect, in the interests not only of the Maritime provinces but of the Dominion as a whole. I realize that the Maritime provinces have been handicapped by difficulties which deserve the fullest consideration of this House, and something must be done to remedy the situation. But we must proceed in the .proper way. We do not want hysterical speeches by hon. gentlemen who one year fix coal rates and two or three years afterwards come to parliament and apply to have these rates altered. We do not want them calling themselves Maritime rigbters and on the vital question of railways standing behind the leader of -the opposition, who is opposed to the Intercolonial being put back in the place where the people of the Maritime provinces want it. That is not the way to get results. Those of us who are anxious to see that part of Canada make progress must look at the facts. There are differences of opinion and there is no reason why these differences should not be inquired into. The government is sympathetic to difficult conditions wherever they exist in any part of this Dominion, and are anxious to devise and to find and apply whatever remedies can be found to make for the unity and upbuilding of Canada.

We have had something in the nature of a confession from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald), when at the outset o'f his statement to-night he declared that the ensuing adjournment would be no holiday for members of the government inasmuch as they would require all the time at their disposal to prepare legislation for submission to parliament when it meets again.
To perfect legislation, I said.

My hon. friend forgets that besides the members of the government there are in this House possibly 230 hon. gentlemen for whom- it will be a holiday, and a holiday to which we object, which we do not ask for, which we do not desire and for which

The Address-Mr. Guthrie
the counrtry will have to pay. It has been charged by the opposition in this House for the last four or five weeks at least that the government had no business to lay before parliament and was not ready to do business. It has been intimated for weeks now, at least since the motion was made for the adjournment, that those on your left, Mr. Speaker, were prepared to get down to business and to vote on the Address at any moment the government would come forward with business to be done. Buit until this moment nothing has been brought forward by the government, and the government now seeks an adjournment practically for its own purposes to prepare legislation against the r.e-assembling of parliament on the 15th. I for one take no exception whatever to the present motion of the government for the application of that parliamentary rule which we know as closure. I was one of those who in the year 1913 voted against the introduction of that rule, but after reflection during the intervening years-
Oh, Oh.

My hon. friends laugh,
but their reflection has taken place only in the last twenty-four hours. In a few hours they have made a complete change of front. After reflection, I say, I have come to the conclusion, which I state wholly on my own authority, that no large deliberative body can operate satisfactorily without some form of closure. I do not believe that the proceedings of this parliament can be properly carried on now or in the future without the reasonable application of the closure rule. All the proceedings in the parliament of Great Britain are conducted practically under closure. It is not formally moved in that House for the reason that there is no necessity for so doing; the rule exists and the Prime Minister merely gives notice that at such and such a time on a certain day the vote will be taken, and the vote is taken accordingly. Closure is the rule in the United States House of Representatives, and1 it is also in our book of rules in this parliament. It should be a rule generally accepted and generally adopted if we in this parliament are going to transact properly the necessary business we are called upon to transact at every session.
Now I do not know that I have any protest whatever to offer. I feel rather like congratulating the government on the step it has taken to-day in moving this motion of closure. It is the first sign of life the government has exhibited for many weeks. It would have been far more to the credit of the government had it taken this step four or
five weeks ago; the present departure suggests not only here but in every part of the country that the government has been driven into a corner and as a last resort has adopted rule 17 which has all the time been on the rule book of the House of Commons. I cannot say I commend the courage of hon. gentlemen opposite in this respect. But there are two kinds of courage, it is true:	There is that
courage that springs from confidence and from manly gallantry, and there is the courage born of fear. Everyone knows that even a coward driven into a corner will show fight; we know, everyone knows, that even a worm will turn if trodden upon. And if I cannot congratulate the government upon the courage it has displayed in this parliament I can at least say that I am heartily glad that as a last resource it has through courage born of fear brought in this measure of closure.
There is no doubt,-you realize it, Mr. Speaker, every thinking man in this House realizes it, and the electors of the Dominion realize it-that for the past eight weeks we have had something like a parliamentary fiasco in the House of Commons. I am not going to place the blame or responsibility for this situation on any party in this House. I am candid enough to say that in my opinion it has resulted from the election 'held on October 29 last. But this parliamentary fiasco might have been avoided, it should have been avoided, and it would have been avoided had the Prime Minister of this country taken the course he should have taken, and which in his Richmond Hill speech he promised to take, when he knew the result of the electoral vote on October 29. All our troubles have their ^ starting point in the unwarranted resolution of the Prime Minister to retain office. From that point our difficulties began to arise and, as time went on, to accumulate and to become greater and Igreater, until at this moment we have what I know I am within the judgment of the House in describing as a practical parliamentary deadlock. I have spoken privately with many hon. members in every quarter of the House, thinking, intelligent and reasonable men. In private conversation in the lobbies or in the rooms of this building there seems to be unanimity of opinion upon this point, that present conditions are not satisfactory, and that they cannot be made satisfactory; that there is only one solution of our present trouble, and the sooner that solution is brought about the better it will be for parliament and the Dominion. That solution is a speedy appeal to the electors of Canada.

The Address-Mr. Guthrie
I do not say it in any language of disrespect, but I tell the government that it has become a by-word and a jest in every city, town and village of the country. Serious people from one end of the Dominion to the other of every shade of political opinion seem to unite in this view, that a situation exists in this House of Commons to-day which can be solved only in one way-by an appeal to the court of last resort; by another appeal to the electors.
You have had two chances to do that.
Let us examine the situation without passion or excitement or ill-feeling.
There is no passion at all.

We have a government
supported by a 'hundred of its followers, faced by an opposition of 116 intelligent, able, *capable, resolute men, an opposition convinced that it is right, and determined to oppose this government because it confidently believes the government is wrong. Then we have another group, or rather several groups, making up a membership of 29. These hon. gentlemen, although divided among themselves, at the present time accord a very general support to the government; but never up to the present moment have they had an opportunity of expressing their confidence, or lack of confidence, in the government. This lack of opportunity has been brought about simply through the skilful manoeuvring and the finesse of the government. True, there was an opportunity in tlhe early days of the session when a straight want of confidence motion was moved, and when a test of strength might have taken place; but no, it was not permitted; a minister of the crown to relieve the government of its difficulty and embarrassment, had solemnly to inform hon. members of the Progressive party that the government would not treat a favourable vote on that motion as a vote of confidence; in short- tlhe minister had to plead with the Progressives to secure their support and avoid a decision on a straight vote of confidence. Since then we have never had an opportunity of moving one; by closure and by moving of the previous question we have been denied that opportunity.
Now, I think everyone must realize that the tenure of office of a government situated as this is is precarious in the extreme. What assurance is there to us or to the people of Canada of any permanence about the situation, or that we will get anything but

haphazard, and sectional legislation at best? What assurance have my hon. friends of the Progressive group that this government, which for four years has resolutely denied their demands, and which now through force of political expediency says, "Hold on, support us, and we will grant your demands"-I say what confidence can the Progressive members have in such a pledge? What confidence can my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) have in a promise made under such circumstances? He has the honour of a front seat and is looked upon as an out and out supporter of the government-though by the way a few months ago he actually opposed a minister of this government and diefeated him. Why is he now one of their supporters? Simply by reason of the fact that he has induced the Prime Minister to write him a personal letter-promising to do what? To amend the criminal code, to amend the Naturalization Act, to amend the Immigration Act-to amend three acts which this government had resolutely refused to touch through the course of four sessions. Why is that promise made now? Simply political expediency again. A government that has to stoop in that way, that has to hold out blandishments and allurements to those hon. members in the left hand comer of this House and to make other promises to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, cannot be more than temporary and makeshift at best.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if the situation is as I have pictured it-and I do not think I have overdrawn it-if my statement meets with the judgment of hon. members, reasonable men in every quarter of the House, what is our duty under the circumstances? Shall we allow the disrespect-the growing disrespect-throughout Canada of parliament and parliamentary institutions to continue and to gather force? Or is it our duty as good, loyal Canadians having respect for this Chamber and for our parliamentary institutions, to seek to solve the problem, no matter if the solution be difficult? It will not be difficult in this case, Sir. My hon. friend the leader of the government (Mr. Lapointe) stated this afternoon the absolute determination of the government to continue in office. We all pass out of this sphere in course of time and our places are very readily

filled; nobody is indispensable. But to continue, I fancy, is the resolution of the Prime Minister. I have been in polities for several years. Now, Mr. Speaker, we sometimes hear that Quebec will become Conservative again. The Quebec people have too much honour to elect any more Tory candidates. In 1917 what did we see in Ontario papers? We saw it stated that "Quebec must not rule," and that "only a solid Ontario could defeat them." That is what we saw, and it was signed by the Tory candidates in the holy city of Toronto. (Mr. Pouliot.]
accept as my supporter a man who would defame 2,500,000 people who are honest and deserving of better than that.

Mr. Speaker, the plenteous showers of congratulations which have fallen upon you during the past two months must now be accompanied by universal regret that it has fallen to you, one of the most highly respected first commoners in the history of our country, to preside over the most unconstitutionally founded parliament, t/he most futile and the
most insincere parliament in our history. It is a parliament, Sir, without a head, a parliament Without a policy, and a parliament existing for one purpose only. The reasons for the Statements, Sir, are very well known. For four years the country has entrusted the administration of its affairs to the Prime Minister and his government, in order that he might implement the promises he made during the election campaign. For four years we have had parliaments of 9 pm.	barter and trade, parliaments
which have existed for nothing else than to sacrifice policies for power. This government, Sir, arranged an opening, but it staged an auction sale. This government	brought in a Speech from
the Throne, but they destroyed every principle, every law, which made the Speech from the Throne possible. They moved an Address in reply to the Sipeech from the Throne, but they destroyed the spirit and the soul of parliament. This action too was taken under the influence of the Prime Minister, who on October 1, 1925, at Moose Jaw made these remarks:

Yes, they moved an Address but they destroyed the institution which their fathers by sacrifice and service had established in this country. The institution which we have always looked up to perhaps more than any other has been that of the recognition that a government not elected at the polls should retire. I am not concerned whether they call the "hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) or the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) or the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) or anybody else to form a government; the one voice spoken by the country on the 29tlh October last was: We do not want the Mackenzie King government. Mr. McINTOSH. You will get it when the time comes. In respect to the question of closure, I believe that, the introduction of closure at the present time can be justified. This House has been in session for two months. We have talked and talked. I believe the general opinion of the country is that all parties in this House have talked too much during the last two months. I believe the wish of the .people of Canada and the verdict of the people of Canada, if you could get it, would be for this government to get down to business.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friends on the other side pound their desks, but I know the thought I am giving expression to is the one that they have in common among themselves, and with their co-operation and the co-operation of all parties it may not be a difficult

The Address-Mr. McMillan
matter to get down to business. I believe the majority should rule, and since I have proved that on every occasion when the vote was taken in this House the ministerial party have had' a majority, we have a perfect-right to introduce closure, to put the clamps on the opposition and1 to say: "Now is the time for this parliament to clear the decks for action, bring down the programme of the government and introduce legislation to carry out that programme."
There is another reason why the closure should be upheld1 at the present time. I believe the Speech from the Throne involves policies which will redound to the glory of Canada, and when we analyze the programme question by question we shall find that the legislation which it foreshadows will prove, when enacted, the best that has been passed in this Dominion during the last quarter of a century. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) not very long ago, in referring to this portion of the House, characterized it as the Saskatchewan colony. Well, I am proud to belong to the province of Saskatchewan; I am proud to come from that sunny part of the Dominion, the land of the west where Canadian development is taking place on such a large scale and where perhaps the destiny of Canada lies to a greater extent than in any other part of the country. Let me tell the right hon. gentleman that, whether the Saskatchewan members constitute a colony in this House or not, that colony has performed a very useful service in supporting this government. Without the support of the members from Saskatchewan it would not be possible for the government to carry on to-day, and I believe that with the combined efforts of Quebec and Saskatchewan, two of the banner provinces of Canada, we can go forward and realize those high ideals of Liberalism and national (progress which will make Canada a great and prosperous nation.
Before I conclude there is just one point I wish to touch upon. From the standpoint of colonial development Saskatchewan has proved most successful. The old Tory idea of colonial development was that Canada existed for the profit of the Motherland; it was a land of snow and ice and of forests, and in the early days at any rate the prevalent notion among Tories was that Canadian development was synonymous with the profit of the empire. We have got beyond that stage of thinking; we are to-day a free nation within the British Empire. Canada, if it is properly developed, has a great future before it. Tories of old had the idea that she would never enjoy the political rights which are hers to-day; but Canada has gone on and prospered, and I
believe that the province of Saskatchewan will play an increasingly important part in the future development of this Dominion.
In closing, may I express the hope that after this test vote is taken to-night and we return to our homes for a week or so we shall come back later on prepared to enact such legislation as will be a credit to this House and to the country as a whole.

In the midst of this river of discussion, "a little nonsense now and then is relished by the best of men". I have heard so many members on the floor of this House say that their homes are in the province of Nova Scotia that I have naturally recalled the occasion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's first visit to the west. He was entertained at Ladner's Landing, on the delta of the Fraser, by a warm friend of my own named William Ladner. In the course of that function, acting as host, he told the gathering which included Sir Wilfrid and another good friend, Mr. D. C. Fraser, afterwards Lieutenant Governor of Nova Scotia, that if they wanted to see the finest country in the world they had only to go outdoors, where they would behold land, that would produce 14,000 bushels of wheat to the acre. Mr. Fraser at once declared, "We had some liars in Nova Scotia but I never knew that any of them had settled here."
In my opinion the application of closure in this discussion has not come before its time. Many of us consider that it was due weeks ago; but possibly it is well that hon. gentlemen opposite have been allowed to go the limit, in an almost continuous exhibition of their policy of obstruction,-a scene, tragic to the Tory party,-a scene deeply expressive, in almost every Tory countenance, of those momentous words, "so near and yet so far". You, Mr. Speaker, may be able to recall the famous expression of a one time respected member of this House, uttered in true Irish brogue, that a Tory out of office was like a she bear deprived of her cubs. Well, Sir, this House has fully demonstrated that the Tory party, at bay on the floor of parliament, is even worse than that. But every unjust accusation, every epithet hurled across the floor in their desperation, both ungenerous and uncalled for, has been met by that feeling which is conscious of the right and that quiet dignity of reserve which will always appeal to the 'best judgment of the House and of the country.
To think that the once great Conservative party, that party which has always plumed itself on the possession of a monopoly in its loyalty to the crown, is now represented by a class of men in this parliament who make

The Address-Mr. McMillan
themselves ridiculous by refusing to allow even an expression of.thanks to the crown for the gracious speech which His Excellency has been pleased to convey to us. At all times it is the difty of every member to uphold and maintain the dignity of parliament. We have seen too much in the public press. Too much has fallen from the lips of hon. gentlemen opposite, who by their words have shown themselves unworthy of those they would revile. Never was any body of independent representatives less open to such sordid charges. These men from the west, both Liberal and Progressive, represent the very soul of honour and they have the highest conception of the duties and responsibilities of their position. As befits the great section of the country from which they come, they are not narrow or circumscribed in their opinions; they are like the rest of us here, endeavouring to do their duty, and in doing so they ally themselves with men of vision, men of high purpose, that together we may maintain Canada on that great highway which will lead to a just realization of the possibilities that lie before us.
Sir, the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) pulled off a good joke the other night in his reference to Mr. Mackenzie King's ability as an angler after Progressive support, and also to the unavailing efforts of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) and the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Rogers), and to the fact that the Hon. Manning Doherty had been down here for a whole month fishing and never got a bite. The hon. member gave Mr. Mackenzie King credit for being the only expert angler in the bunch. But, Sir, one weakness of the hon. gentleman's reference lies in the fact that he did not go far enough; he did not complete the picture; if he had done so, the mystery would have vanished, and the whole picture would be as clear as the noonday sun. When these hon. gentlemen were busy fishing they were not fishing for themselves, they were fishing for their leader, the right hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), and in their sport they mistook the calibre of their game. They thought the Progressives were men of their own calibre, and so they loaded their hooks with Arthur Meighen-Hugh Guthrie-Bob Rogers^Manning Doherty bait. But it was the wrong kind of bait. No wonder they dropped their fishing in disgust. They now know to their sorrow that they might have fished till doomsday and never have caught any of the fish they were after with that bait. Mr. Mackenzie King had nothing to do with the fishing. His only duty was to provide the right kind of bait. It was the leader of 
the House (Mr. Lapointe) who loaded his hook with the right kind of bait, with "Mackenzie King bait," otherwise known as the "best-interests-of-Canada" bait. And he went off in his own jolly way, and1 by his continuously overflowing good nature was able not only to squash the opposition but to captivate this House so that he has to-day behind him and across the way more loyal support than any government has had in years, a support that will be continued so long as the government do their duty. It is the earnest hope, it is the feeling deep down in the heart of every member on this side of the House, including the members of the cabinet, that the government will go forward and do their duty-do it as they have done in days gone by, with honour to themselves and benefit to the country.
